title: The world Church
hookLine: the Catholic Church's center of gravity shifts toward Latin America, Africa and Asia

lines: A NIGERIAN PRIEST IN THE MIDWEST.
cards: Some Sunday mornings now look like this. In a small town in the American Midwest, the priest at the altar grew up in Nigeria. In a parish in Ireland, the homily comes in the accent of southern India.

In Kinshasa, a choir comes up the aisle dancing, with drums. In Manila, the doors are open because the crowd won't fit inside. And in Rome, the last two popes came from Buenos Aires and from a missionary life in Peru.
Same Mass, same prayers, many languages.

teach.b: The Creed at Mass calls the Church catholic, and the Catechism says plainly what that means: universal. A church for everyone, everywhere.
For long stretches of history, though, the center of Catholic life sat in Europe: its bishops, its universities, the missionaries it sent out. That picture has changed.

teach.h: A CENTER OF GRAVITY MOVING SOUTH.
teach.b: Writers who follow the Church describe its center of gravity moving south, toward Latin America, Africa and Asia, and they point to the Church's own yearly statistics to show it.
Catholics read their oldest texts as pointing this way from the start. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sends the apostles out: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations."
And at Pentecost, in Acts, the crowd in Jerusalem is Jews gathered from far and wide, "devout men, out of every nation under heaven," each hearing the apostles in his own language.
Some readers call Pentecost the Church's birthday: a church that spoke many languages on its first day. The shift isn't a tidy story.

teach.h: GOING THEREFORE, TEACH YE ALL NATIONS.
teach.b: In some places the faith arrived with missionaries who traveled alongside colonial powers, and that history includes real harm, which the Church has had to face.
But the faith also spread through local catechists, mothers and grandmothers, and converts who made it their own and sang it to their own music.

Today the traffic runs in every direction: African and Asian priests serve European parishes, Latin American theologians are read in seminaries far away, and bishops from every continent sit together at synods in Rome.

how: Catholics celebrate the same Mass in many languages and musical styles, and some parishes in Europe and North America are served by priests and religious sisters from Africa, Asia and Latin America.

practice: Let one face or city in Africa come to mind, a whole continent, not one place: a priest you've met, a choir you've heard, a country known only from a map.

Picture a parish there getting ready for Sunday: someone sweeping the floor, someone tuning a drum, a catechist walking in from a village. If you pray, pray for that parish and its people; if you don't, simply wish them well.
